  1   I.      INTRODUCTION

 2           When denying Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss, the Court allowed Defendants to conduct

 3   limited discovery into the question of whether Plaintiff “actually rel[ied] on the initial display

 4   price of the chairs that she purchased from World Market when she purchased them,” and to

 5   move for summary judgment if there was “no genuine dispute of fact as to Harvey’s reliance.”

 6   Defendants now seek summary judgment, contending that discovery “conclusively establishes”

 7   Plaintiff did not rely on the initial display price of the Jarle Chair Set.

 8           Plaintiff did, in fact, rely on the initial advertised price when deciding to purchase the
 9   chairs. Plaintiff had a budget of $500 when purchasing patio furniture. While shopping online,
10   Plaintiff, like all online shoppers, was exposed to hundreds with possible options—she was
11   presented with hundreds of outdoor furniture options on World Market’s site alone. Yet, during
12   her search, she only clicked on products advertised for less than $500. When Plaintiff clicked on
13   the Jarle Chair Set, it was advertised for $429.99. Plaintiff committed to purchase the Chair Set
14   because she thought the chairs were $429.99—within her budget. After she found out the chairs
15   would cost $529.94—outside her budget—she vacillated but ultimately decided to go forward
16   because she did not want to spend more time looking for a chair set. As Plaintiff’s expert
17   explains, this type of scenario is precisely why businesses delay the disclosure of the true cost of
18   their wares. The unlawful practice of drip pricing lures consumers who otherwise would not have

19   considered a product and causes them to pay more than they otherwise would have been willing

20   to spend. Plaintiff has testified that she initially considered the Jarle Chair Set because it was

21   listed as costing under $500, and would not have committed to the Chair Set had she learned

22   immediately that the Chair Set cost over $500.

23           Further, Plaintiff does not need to show she relied on the initial display price to prevail on

24   any of her claims. The Consumers Legal Remedies Act (“CLRA”), Unfair Competition Law

25   (“UCL”), and False Advertising Law (“FAL”) all require Plaintiff to show she was injured “as a

26   result of” a prohibited practice. The California Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that

27   reliance is just one means of showing causation, and that reliance is only necessary if a plaintiff

28   proceeds under a theory that she was defrauded, because “reliance is the causal mechanism of
                                                   1

  1   fraud.” Drip pricing is an unlawful practice that harms consumers even when consumers know

 2   they are not being told the full price upfront, and Plaintiff specifically was harmed “as a result of”

 3   World Market’s use of drip pricing regardless of whether she specifically relied on the veracity of

 4   the initial advertised price. First, Plaintiff can prove she was charged a higher price because of

 5   Defendants’ delayed disclosure of the full price. As Plaintiff’s expert, Prof. Sebastien Bradley,

 6   explains, drip pricing provides businesses with a market advantage: more consumers consider

 7   their goods because they appear cheaper than they in fact are. Prof. Bradley’s research has found

 8   that when businesses are forced to stop using drip pricing, they actually lower their prices. And he
 9   opines that had World Market complied with the law, it would have likely reduced the price of the
10   Chair Set to remain competitive. Second, because World Market did not properly advertise its
11   mandatory fees, those fees were illegal, and Plaintiff was harmed by paying those unlawful fees.
12   For the CLRA claim, Plaintiff can show yet additional injuries: World Market wasted Plaintiff’s
13   time by making it more difficult for her to find the true price of the Chair Set, a form of
14   transactional cost, and World Market’s tactics diverted her from finding a better possible deal, an
15   opportunity cost. Because Harvey can show she suffered harm “as a result of” Defendants’
16   practice through these many routes, summary judgment cannot be granted.
17   II.    PROCEDURAL HISTORY
18          Plaintiff filed this lawsuit on October 3, 2024. Dkt. 1-3. The Second Amended Complaint

19   was filed on February 2, 2025. Dkt. 1-25. She has brought claims on behalf of herself, a class of

20   similarly situated persons, and the general public against Defendants based on violations of the

21   Consumers Legal Remedies Act (“CLRA”), Cal. Civ. Code § 1750, et seq., which prohibits

22   companies from “offering a price for a good or service that does not include all mandatory fees or

23   charges,” with the exception of certain government-imposed charges and “[p]ostage or carriage

24   charges that will be reasonably and actually incurred.” Cal. Civ. Code § 1770(a)(29). See also id.

25   at § 1770(a)(9). She has also brought claims under the Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), Bus. &

26   Prof. Code § 17200, et seq., which prohibits the use of drip pricing as an unfair and unlawful

 8          To prevail on their motion, Defendants must “show[] that there is no genuine dispute as to
 9   any material fact” and that they are “entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P.
10   56(a); see also Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322 (1986). Under this standard, summary
11   judgment must only be entered “if, under the governing law, there can be but one reasonable
12   conclusion as to the verdict.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 250 (1986). A
13   genuine dispute as to a material fact exists “if the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could
14   return a verdict for the nonmoving party.” Anderson, 477 U.S. at 248. “[I]f the nonmoving party
15   produces enough evidence to create a genuine issue of material fact,” the motion cannot be
16   granted. Nissan Fire & Marine Ins. Co., Ltd. v. Fritz Cos., Inc., 210 F.3d 1099, 1103 (9th Cir.
17   2000). The Court must view all inferences drawn from the underlying facts in the light most
18   favorable to the nonmoving party. Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S.

19   574, 587 (1986). Summary judgment is therefore not appropriate “where contradictory inferences

20   may reasonably be drawn from undisputed evidentiary facts.” Hollingsworth Solderless Terminal

21   Co. v. Turley, 622 F.2d 1324, 1335 (9th Cir. 1980). If evidence produced by the moving party

22   conflicts with evidence produced by the nonmoving party, the Court must assume the truth of the

23   evidence set forth by the nonmoving party with respect to that fact. See Leslie v. Grupo ICA, 198

24   F.3d 1152, 1158 (9th Cir. 1999). Nor can the Court make credibility determinations regarding the

25   evidence offered on summary judgment. See T.W. Elec. Serv., Inc. v. Pac. Elec. Contractors

26   Ass’n, 809 F.2d 626, 630-31 (9th Cir. 1987) (citing Matsushita, 475 U.S. at 587).
